issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: For a toxic chemical exposure trauma, water/flooding/large bodies of water is a poor fit as a trauma cue unless there is specific contamination-through-water context, which is not reflected anywhere else in the profile. The other items suggest generalized danger and intrusive memory, not a flood/water-based trauma context, so this trigger is hard to explain clinically.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships
issues.explanation: Avoiding new friendships or relationships is not well linked to the rest of the formulation. The profile centers on toxic exposure, hypervigilant threat monitoring, intrusive memories, and self-devaluation/hopelessness, but contains no interpersonal threat, mistrust, shame, or relationship-focused appraisals that would make this strategy a coherent consequence. It appears to target a symptom domain not otherwise represented in the selected items.

For toxic chemical exposure, hospital/antiseptic smell and darkness/nighttime can plausibly cue the event or its aftermath, but 'Known People: Related people' is hard to justify unless the trauma centrally involved family members. Nothing else in the profile suggests interpersonal betrayal, family-linked danger, or family members as part of the exposure, so this trigger appears poorly matched to the trauma type and the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
issues.explanation: The negative appraisals are heavily global and depressive/existential ('Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore', 'I have no future') rather than trauma-linked threat/self-appraisals. In this formulation Negative Appraisals has a very strong link to Threat, but the threat items are about persistent danger/vigilance in unfamiliar places. 'Can't rely on myself' fits that pattern; the meaninglessness/hopelessness items do not connect well to the toxic exposure theme, the selected triggers, or the specific threat content, making the node less coherent.

vignette:
Somsak is a 66-year-old roofer who has been married for over forty years. He came to therapy at his wife’s urging, though he is not sure what talking can do now. The event that changed everything happened three years ago, when he was called to repair a leak on the roof of a small industrial cleaning facility. The job seemed straightforward, but as he worked near a vent, a cloud of chemical fumes rose and engulfed him. He remembers the smell vividly—sharp, sweet, and metallic, like antiseptic mixed with something burning. His throat closed, his eyes streamed, and he could not breathe. He crawled to the edge of the roof, gasping, certain he was going to die right there. A coworker called an ambulance, and Somsak spent three days in the hospital on oxygen. The doctors said his lungs were irritated but not permanently damaged. He was sent home with instructions to rest.

He did not rest. Instead, he found that he could not stop replaying the moment the fumes hit him. The memory is like a film that plays over and over in his mind, always the same sequence: the vent, the smell, the panic, the feeling of his lungs seizing. Sometimes, without any clear image, the full emotional intensity of the event washes over him—the terror, the suffocation—and he is left shaking, unable to understand why. The memory itself is very clear and detailed, more vivid than anything else in his life. He can still taste the chemical on his tongue.

The smell became a trap. Any antiseptic scent, any hospital or clinic waiting room, triggers the same physical response. Worse, he discovered that related smells—cleaning products, paint thinner, even strong air fresheners—can do it too. He now avoids going to the doctor altogether, which worries his wife because of his age. But what frightens Somsak most is the dark. Nighttime, or waking up in the dark, brings the memory rushing back. He cannot say why, but the darkness feels like the blindness of that moment when the fumes clouded his vision. He has come to believe that he cannot rely on himself anymore. Before the event, he was a competent man who could fix anything. Now he is certain the world is a dangerous place, and that he is not equipped to handle it. He feels he has no future.

His avoidance has become a way of life. He no longer goes anywhere unfamiliar, because he cannot assess the danger. He sticks to the same routes, the same stores, the same few rooms in his house. At work, he used to be the one who spoke up about safety concerns. Now he never disagrees or asserts himself, to avoid any conflict that might escalate into something unpredictable. He tries hard not to think about the trauma at all, pushing the memories down, but they surface anyway, especially at night. He dwells constantly on how he used to be before the event—active, confident, unafraid. That man feels lost to him.

The consequences have been concrete. He was given light duty after the incident, but his concentration has suffered. On the roof, he finds himself unable to focus, his mind drifting to the smell or the darkness, and he has made small errors that could have been dangerous. His supervisor has noticed. Somsak is terrified of being let go, but he cannot explain why he is struggling. At home, he is unable to relax even when he knows he is safe. He sits rigidly in his chair, scanning the room, waiting for something bad to happen. His wife has stopped asking him to go out for dinner or to visit their grandchildren, because he always says no. She is patient, but Somsak sees the worry in her eyes, and it makes him feel worse.

What finally brought him here was a night last month when he woke up in the dark, gasping, certain he was back on that roof. He could not catch his breath for several minutes. His wife held him and said, quietly, that she could not watch him suffer like this anymore. Somsak agreed to come, though he is not sure what he is hoping for. He is most afraid that nothing will work, and that he will spend the rest of his years trapped in this small, fearful life. But somewhere, beneath the hopelessness, there is a faint wish to feel like himself again, even if he cannot imagine what that would look like.
